overview: Zengi was the Turkic ruler of Mosul and Aleppo whose capture of Edessa in 1144 shocked the Latin east and helped provoke the Second Crusade.
Zengi is remembered as a precursor of later Muslim counter-crusade leadership, though his career was also deeply concerned with rivalry among Muslim powers.

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Zengi was the Turkic ruler of Mosul and Aleppo whose capture of Edessa in 1144 shocked the Latin east and helped provoke the Second Crusade.

contentSections.title: Birth and early life
paragraphs: Zengi rose in the Seljuk and atabeg political world, where military households, city control, and nominal loyalty to greater rulers could produce powerful regional dynasties.

contentSections.title: Character and Personality
paragraphs: Imad ad-Din Zengi is remembered as a fierce, hard-driving warlord whose ruthlessness made him the first great Muslim counterforce to the crusader states. The Arabic sources present a commander of severe discipline and explosive temper — feared by his own troops as much as by his enemies — who held his army to harsh order and pursued power in Syria and the Jazira with relentless ambition.

His capture of the crusader county of Edessa in 1144, the first major reversal of the First Crusade's conquests, made him a hero of the counter-crusade in later Muslim memory and provoked the Second Crusade in response. The sources admire his effectiveness while not concealing his cruelty; he was assassinated by his own servants, a fitting end for a ruler who governed through fear.

The portrait is of a brutal but formidable founder of a dynasty, whose violence was inseparable from his success. He is remembered as the hard man who first showed that the crusaders could be rolled back — admired in the Muslim tradition for the blow he struck at Edessa, and acknowledged even by sympathetic sources as a commander as ruthless toward his own as toward his foes.

contentSections.title: As ruler of Mosul and Aleppo
paragraphs: Zengi built power across northern Syria and Mesopotamia, using military pressure and political calculation against Muslim rivals as well as the crusader states. His capture of Edessa was the first major fall of a crusader state.

contentSections.title: Death
paragraphs: Zengi was assassinated in 1146 by a servant while campaigning, leaving his domains divided between his sons, including Nur ad-Din.

contentSections.title: Legacy
paragraphs: Zengi is remembered as a precursor of later Muslim counter-crusade leadership, though his career was also deeply concerned with rivalry among Muslim powers.

timeline.title: Born
timeline.description: Zengi was born into the military-political world of the Seljuk successor states.

timeline.title: Takes Mosul
timeline.description: Control of Mosul gave him a major base in northern Mesopotamia.

timeline.title: Gains Aleppo
timeline.description: Aleppo linked him directly to Syrian politics and the crusader frontier.

timeline.title: Captures Edessa
timeline.description: The fall of Edessa transformed crusader-state security and provoked western alarm.

timeline.title: Assassinated
timeline.description: Zengi’s death passed his legacy to Nur ad-Din.

predecessor.displayName: None as founder of the Zengid state
predecessor.note: Zengi received Mosul as governor for the Seljuk sultan in 1127 and built an independent dynasty from it

successor.note: His son took Aleppo; another son, Saif ad-Din, took Mosul
